title: Vampire Planet: How Capitalism Chokes Los Angeles
author: Joshua Frank
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/FB440226-CF9B-42A0-9492-854089A4C013-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/vampire-
planet-how-capitalism-chokes-los-angeles/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/FB440226-CF9B-42A0-9492-854089A4C013-680x510.jpeg)

Port of Los Angeles, photograph by Joshua Frank.

It’s a balmy evening in San Pedro, California. I’m standing on the outskirts
of a Little League ballpark atop a knoll, overlooking the arching Vincent St.
Thomas Bridge. Below, a sea of shipping containers from the Port of LA and
Long Beach are stacked high like Lego blocks, forming mini-skyscrapers along
the dusky horizon. Together, these two ports handle 40% of all containerized
imports into the United States. It’s a mammoth, sprawling complex spanning 24
square miles.

It’s also one of the largest sources of pollution in the LA area.

Cargo ships themselves emit a lot of emissions. A single container ship emits
up to 5 metric tons of CO2 per hour while at port. Together, the Long Beach
and LA ports handle an average of 40 ships per day. Port traffic and idling
ships cause more than [2,400 deaths per
year.](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/classic/ch/communities/ra/westoakland/documents/reduction.pdf)
In West Long Beach, which inhales the majority of the pollution emitted from
the port, life expectancy is [8 years
lower](https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/11/la-long-beach-ports-
pollution/) than in wealthier areas in LA County.

Thanks to the port’s operations and the ships and trucks it handles, this area
is now known as the “diesel-death zone.”

The 20-mile-long 710 freeway, which serves as the main transport artery for
the vast LA-Long Beach port complex. It’s a massive highway packed full of
thundering semi-trucks nearly every hour of the day.

With their horns belching and tires screeching, the constant hum of big rigs
can be heard for miles. This stretch of the 710 is one of the deadliest roads
in the nation, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety
Administration. A [2013 Vox report](https://www.vox.com/a/deadliest-
interstates-united-states) showed that only Interstate 285 in Georgia ranked
higher. It makes perfect sense. I was recently told a gruesome tale from a
grieving father who lost his son after his motorcycle was sucked under a semi-
truck that was racing down the freeway at 70 mph. His bike was pulverized, and
the 19-year-old kid died instantly. [![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-18-at-1.11.49-PM.png)](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/UfU8gx4LO98oZP-
hvrl3zQ)

These horrific events occur all too frequently. Even large SUVs don’t stand a
chance against a Mack truck pulling a 50,000-pound load. The remedy, at least
the one proposed by the region’s judicious transportation authorities, is to
widen the freeway to reduce traffic bottlenecks and accident risk. Much to the
highway lobby’s chagrin, a $6 billion project to expand the 710 was shot down
in May 2022 after 15 years of planning. Local advocates fought hard, rightly
pointing out that poor communities of color would be most affected by the
development.

“Though it took way too long to get a commitment to prioritize health and
well-being, our community embraces this decision as a victory,” said Laura
Cortez, co-director, East Yard Communities for Environmental Justice, a member
of the 710 Task Force opposition. “However, the 710 as it is now causes
significant harm daily, and community members along the 710 will continue to
work so community voices are prioritized, and we don’t replicate the harms of
the previous process.”

Nearly 1.2 million people live in neighborhoods that hug the hectic 710, 83%
of whom are Black and Latinx, and the air they inhale is among the most toxic
in the country. The EPA
[estimates](https://archive.epa.gov/region9/strategicplan/web/html/i710.html)
the area accounts for nearly 20% of all particulate-laden diesel emissions in
Southern California, and the toll on human health is insurmountable.

Living in a haze of diesel exhaust, as you might imagine, harms health,
especially for children who are still developing. The pollution is visible
nearly everywhere you look, caking the sides of buildings and covering cars
with soot if they sit in one place long enough. The USC Environmental Health
Center notes that people living in areas like the 710 corridor are more likely
to experience premature births and have higher rates of heart disease, asthma,
and lung cancer. While the greater Los Angeles area continues to rank among
the worst air-quality regions in the country, hotspots in LA County
consistently appear along the 710 freeway.

Trump’s tariffs haven’t slowed port traffic, mainly because importers have
been scrambling to stock up on goods before prices rise. The ports recorded
the [second-highest level](https://portoflosangeles.org/references/2026-news-
releases/news_081826_july_cargo) of imports in July, and August appears to be
on a similar track. This means more ships and more truck traffic on the 710,
and, ultimately, a hell of a lot more pollution.

This past week, the Port of Long Beach announced it had [signed a
deal](https://www.cbsnews.com/losangeles/news/port-of-long-beach-signs-deal-
to-build-small-offshore-nuclear-reactors/) to build a small modular nuclear
reactor that would float on barges. The proposal is unlikely to go anywhere,
as significant hurdles remain, and cost is only one of them. There’s a 1976
ban on nuclear energy construction in California, and while SMR technology
isn’t new, putting one of these reactors on a floating platform in the middle
of a busy port complex is novel, risky business.

I reached out to my friend and nuclear expert MV Ramana, who wrote the
fantastic book [_Nuclear Is Not the
Solution_](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/c_Q0CGOT0rQmcdezkwGD8w) ,
to see what he made of the announcement that the port was looking at nuclear.
He didn’t seem all that worried.

“There has been talk about SMRs, and nuclear reactors more generally, powering
ships for decades. The Savannah, the first nuclear-powered ship, was launched
back in 1959, and officials described it as ‘potentially the greatest
revolution in maritime history,’ said Ramana. “But it quickly became apparent
that it cost too much to operate, and the ship has been moved to storage in
Baltimore harbor. Nuclear reactors, if anything, have become more expensive
than in the 1950s.”

A far more reasonable solution to some of the port’s pollution is wind energy.
The Port of Long Beach is planning to construct a large, 400-acre, $4.7
billion wind farm called Pier Wind that will produce 25 gigawatts of offshore
wind energy by 2045, enough to electrify 25 million homes. But unlike the SMR
plan, that energy isn’t being built to power port operations, it’s meant to
feed the grid itself.

As for all the pollution the port is producing now, from those big ships to
the dirty trucks, there’s nothing in the works that will radically reduce
emissions any time soon (aside from a [meager
push](https://portoflosangeles.org/references/2024-news-
releases/news_062724_pola_polb_truck_charging) to electrify trucking fleets).
The poor folks near the port and along the 710 corridor will keep paying the
price for an economic system reliant on cheap imports from faraway lands.
